questions.question: A patient has an established symptomatic HF syndrome and reproducible LVEF of 46%. There is no previous lower EF measurement. How is this phenotype classified under the ESC 2026 HF guideline?
options: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Heart failure with improved ejection fraction
questions.explanation:
EF Classification Must Specify the Guideline Framework

Correct answer: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Guideline-Specific Phenotypes

**ESC 2026 defines reduced-EF HF using LVEF ==below 50%== and preserved-EF HF using LVEF ==at least 50%==.** The previous separate mildly reduced group is incorporated into reduced-EF HF.

The AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 framework instead labels EF ≤40% as reduced, 41%–49% as mildly reduced and ≥50% as preserved. Naming the framework prevents two defensible labels from competing in an undated question.

EF classification is applied after establishing the clinical syndrome. A low measurement alone does not establish current symptomatic HF.

Phenotype Is Different From Treatment Eligibility

**A changed phenotype boundary does not rewrite the eligibility criteria of every historical trial or device recommendation.** Preserve the actual EF thresholds and clinical conditions attached to each therapy.

Review symptom burden, congestion, etiology, renal function, rhythm and the EF trajectory. Measurement variability matters near a boundary, particularly when the result would alter a consequential decision.

Do not infer improved EF without a baseline or describe a patient as cured from a reassuring single scan. Document both the measured value and the guideline used so a classification update does not create ambiguity in the clinical record.

Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction: This is the 41%–49% category in the AHA 2022 and older ESC frameworks. ESC 2026 removed that separate phenotype and includes this EF within reduced-EF HF.

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: ESC 2026 retains preserved EF at 50% or more; 46% does not meet that numerical boundary, even though it may be described informally as only mildly impaired.

Heart failure with improved ejection fraction: Improved EF requires a documented prior reduced value and a subsequent rise under the applicable definition. A single EF of 46% does not demonstrate an improving trajectory.

ESC heart failure guideline, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag100

ESC official summary of HF guideline changes, 2026 — https://www.escardio.org/news/press/press-releases/major-changes-made-to-the-esc-guidelines-on-heart-failure/

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

questions.question: A patient previously treated for symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy had LVEF 28%. After treatment, LVEF is 52% and symptoms have resolved. Under AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 terminology, which classification best preserves the clinical history?
options: Newly diagnosed HF with preserved EF
Heart failure with improved ejection fraction
Pre-HF without a history of symptomatic HF
Persistently reduced-EF HF under the AHA 2022 EF boundary
questions.explanation:
Improved EF Describes a Trajectory Rather Than Cure

Correct answer: Heart failure with improved ejection fraction

Apply the Named Definition

**AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 defines HFimpEF as previous LVEF ≤40% with a subsequent measurement above 40%.** This patient meets both the baseline and follow-up conditions.

The definition does not require the follow-up EF to exceed 50%, although it does here. Other consensus definitions may include an absolute improvement requirement, so do not silently merge definitions.

A single preserved-EF measurement without a prior reduced value would not establish this trajectory.

Continue Longitudinal Care

**Improved EF indicates treatment response or remission, not proof that the substrate and relapse risk have disappeared.** Continue indicated HF therapy even when symptoms resolve, unless a specific contraindication requires adjustment.

Review etiology, rhythm, ventricular dimensions, treatment tolerance and recurrent symptoms. Reassess imaging when clinically indicated rather than stopping follow-up after one favorable result.

Counsel against unsupervised withdrawal of medicines. Decisions about an existing device, arrhythmic risk or future pregnancy require their own assessment and cannot be settled by this classification alone. Documenting the earlier EF also helps avoid inappropriate transfer into a de novo HFpEF treatment pathway that disregards why ventricular function improved.

Newly diagnosed HF with preserved EF: The current EF is preserved numerically, but this label loses the documented reduced-EF trajectory. HFimpEF identifies improvement from the previous reduced value.

Pre-HF without a history of symptomatic HF: Pre-HF describes patients without current or prior HF symptoms/signs who have relevant structural or biomarker abnormalities; it does not erase an established previous symptomatic syndrome.

Persistently reduced-EF HF under the AHA 2022 EF boundary: The current EF exceeds the AHA reduced-EF boundary. Persisting disease risk justifies continued care, but does not make the current EF remain 28% or negate the improved-EF category.

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

questions.question: An adult with hypertension has never experienced HF symptoms or signs. Echocardiography reproducibly shows LV dilation and LVEF 35%. Under AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 staging, which category applies?
options: Stage D: advanced heart failure
Stage A: at risk for heart failure
Stage C: symptomatic heart failure
Stage B: pre-heart failure
questions.explanation:
Asymptomatic Structural Disease Is Pre-Heart Failure

Correct answer: Stage B: pre-heart failure

Separate Stage From EF and Functional Class

**HF stage incorporates disease evolution and symptom history.** Stage B identifies an opportunity to prevent progression before a symptomatic syndrome develops.

Structural abnormalities, impaired ventricular systolic function or evidence of increased filling pressure can establish pre-HF when symptoms/signs are absent. At-risk patients with qualifying persistent biomarker elevation can also meet the framework after competing causes are excluded.

NYHA class describes functional limitation in established symptomatic HF and is not a substitute for the stage A–D framework. An EF category alone also does not determine stage.

Act on the Underlying Abnormality

**Asymptomatic LV systolic dysfunction requires etiological evaluation and preventive treatment rather than reassurance from the absence of dyspnea.** Assess ischemia when appropriate, valve disease, cardiotoxic exposure, rhythm and familial disease.

The AHA 2022 framework recommends ACE inhibition and evidence-based beta blockade in appropriate patients with LVEF ≤40% to prevent symptomatic HF; prior MI creates additional secondary-prevention considerations.

Control blood pressure, review harmful drugs and arrange follow-up of function and symptoms. Do not apply every symptomatic-HFrEF trial regimen indiscriminately to all stage-B phenotypes. Conversely, a patient with previous symptomatic HF who improves on treatment does not revert to never-symptomatic pre-HF solely because today’s examination is normal.

Stage D: advanced heart failure: Stage D concerns advanced, difficult-to-control symptomatic disease despite treatment. A low EF alone does not establish refractory symptoms or an advanced-HF trajectory.

Stage A: at risk for heart failure: Stage A covers risk factors without structural or functional disease or qualifying biomarker abnormalities. Demonstrated LV dilation and systolic dysfunction move this patient beyond risk alone.

Stage C: symptomatic heart failure: Stage C requires current or previous HF symptoms/signs with structural disease. Reduced EF is important but does not supply a symptom history that the vignette explicitly excludes.

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

questions.question: An adult with BMI 42 kg/m² presents with abrupt severe dyspnea and orthopnea. NT-proBNP is 240 pg/mL and lung ultrasound shows diffuse bilateral B-lines. Respiratory stabilization is underway. Which investigation best resolves the discordance between the peptide result and suspected cardiac congestion?
options: Repeat NT-proBNP after six hours before selecting cardiac imaging
Prompt echocardiography integrated with the bedside assessment
High-resolution chest CT as the next definitive test
Spirometry with bronchodilator testing after oxygenation improves
questions.explanation:
A Low Natriuretic Peptide Does Not Override High Clinical Suspicion

Correct answer: Prompt echocardiography integrated with the bedside assessment

Use the Correct Setting and Test

**Natriuretic peptides support probability assessment; they do not replace clinical evaluation.** NT-proBNP below 300 pg/mL is a conventional non-age-adjusted rule-out threshold in acute/decompensated presentations.

Obesity can reduce concentrations. Flash pulmonary edema and selected right-sided or advanced presentations can also have unexpectedly low values, so a low result should not end evaluation when suspicion remains high.

Age, AF and kidney dysfunction can increase values without proving left-sided HF. Bilateral B-lines indicate an interstitial syndrome but are not themselves uniquely cardiogenic.

Reconcile the Discordant Findings

**Assess oxygenation, perfusion, examination and focused imaging promptly.** Echocardiography evaluates ventricular function, valve lesions and filling-pressure evidence while alternative pulmonary causes are considered.

For reference, ESC 2021 conventional nonacute rule-out values were NT-proBNP <125 pg/mL or BNP <35 pg/mL; acute values were NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL or BNP <100 pg/mL. These are different clinical pathways, not interchangeable confirmation thresholds.

ESC 2026 also discusses suggested age-adjusted outpatient NT-proBNP levels above which HF is likely: 125 pg/mL in younger adults under 50, 250 pg/mL at ages 50–75 years and 500 pg/mL in older adults over 75. These outpatient likelihood thresholds are not the acute rule-out pathway and do not independently confirm HF. Do not delay necessary respiratory support while resolving a discordant biomarker result.

Repeat NT-proBNP after six hours before selecting cardiac imaging: Serial peptides may provide context, but obesity and abrupt pulmonary edema can lower concentrations. Repeating the same biomarker should not postpone imaging when clinical suspicion remains substantial.

High-resolution chest CT as the next definitive test: Chest CT can characterize interstitial lung disease or another pulmonary abnormality when that phenotype is suspected. Abrupt orthopnea and B-lines with an unreliable exclusion biomarker first warrant direct cardiac structural and functional assessment.

Spirometry with bronchodilator testing after oxygenation improves: Spirometry helps evaluate chronic obstructive airflow disease when the history and examination support it. It does not promptly resolve an acute cardiac-congestion question and can be difficult to interpret during decompensation.

ESC heart failure guideline, 2021: conventional diagnostic thresholds — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab368

ESC heart failure guideline, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag100

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

questions.question: A patient with unexplained exertional dyspnea has LVEF 62%, no important valve disease and normal pulmonary function testing. Expert supine exercise catheterization reproduces symptoms. Which PAWP pattern meets the invasive HFpEF criterion in the original HFA–PEFF framework?
options: Rest 14 mmHg; peak exercise 24 mmHg
Rest 11 mmHg; peak exercise 23 mmHg
Rest 11 mmHg; peak exercise 29 mmHg
Rest 10 mmHg; peak exercise 20 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Exercise Filling Pressure Can Establish HFpEF Despite Normal Resting Pressure

Correct answer: Rest 11 mmHg; peak exercise 29 mmHg

Demonstrate the Physiological Abnormality

**HFpEF requires a compatible syndrome with objective evidence of abnormal cardiac filling pressures or associated structural/functional abnormalities.** Normal resting pressures do not exclude an exercise-limited phenotype.

The HFA–PEFF framework uses resting ==PAWP ≥15 mmHg== or ==LVEDP ≥16 mmHg== as invasive evidence. In the specified supine exercise setting, peak ==PAWP ≥25 mmHg== supports the diagnosis.

The correct option’s 29-mmHg exercise value crosses that threshold while the resting value remains below 15 mmHg. Interpret a properly acquired result in the context of reproduced symptoms and alternative causes rather than as an isolated number.

Acquisition and Interpretation Limits

**Body position, respiratory pressure swings, workload and measurement technique affect invasive exercise interpretation.** Confirm catheter position, waveform validity and a representative wedge recording.

Do not transfer a supine peak-pressure threshold indiscriminately to every upright protocol. Pressure–flow relationships and the overall hemodynamic pattern can provide additional information in specialist assessment.

Review ischemia, pericardial disease, pulmonary pathology and chronotropic limitation when clinically relevant. Establishing HFpEF should lead to phenotype-directed management and comorbidity assessment, rather than stopping at a normal EF label. Conversely, an elevated wedge does not establish a specific myocardial etiology or mean every dyspneic patient needs invasive testing; use it when noninvasive evaluation leaves consequential uncertainty.

Rest 14 mmHg; peak exercise 24 mmHg: Both values are close to the relevant boundaries but remain below them. Borderline findings require attention to technique and the full clinical context rather than rounding measurements upward to force a diagnosis.

Rest 11 mmHg; peak exercise 23 mmHg: The resting value is below 15 mmHg and the supine exercise value is below 25 mmHg. This pair does not meet the cited absolute-pressure criterion, although a full physiological assessment may still identify other abnormalities.

Rest 10 mmHg; peak exercise 20 mmHg: Exercise normally increases flow and can raise filling pressure. This pattern remains below the original supine exercise threshold and does not independently establish HFpEF by that criterion.

HFA–PEFF diagnostic consensus, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz641

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

questions.question: An ambulatory patient with unexplained exertional dyspnea and preserved EF has a correctly calculated H2FPEF score of 8. There is no important valve lesion. What does this score most appropriately indicate?
options: An intermediate probability in the original diagnostic framework
A high estimated probability of HFpEF that should be integrated with the clinical and cardiac assessment
A high predicted risk of developing HFpEF over the next five years
Invasive confirmation of HFpEF equivalent to an abnormal exercise wedge pressure
questions.explanation:
H2FPEF Estimates Probability Rather Than Replacing Clinical Assessment

Correct answer: A high estimated probability of HFpEF that should be integrated with the clinical and cardiac assessment

Understand the Derivation Question

**H2FPEF combines six clinical and echocardiographic predictors to estimate HFpEF likelihood in patients with unexplained dyspnea.** The original study used invasive exercise assessment to distinguish HFpEF from noncardiac dyspnea.

AF contributes three points and obesity two; the remaining four variables contribute one each. The total ranges from zero to nine.

A high score is useful evidence but does not exclude an alternative or concurrent explanation for symptoms. Its calibration depends on the population in which it is applied.

Use Probability to Guide Evaluation

**Scores of 0–1 suggest low probability, 2–5 intermediate probability and 6–9 high probability in the original framework.** Intermediate or discordant presentations often need additional functional assessment.

Do not confuse this score with HFA–PEFF, which uses different domains, point assignment and decision boundaries. A high H2FPEF value does not automatically imply a high score in the other system.

Check that each component was measured correctly, especially estimated PASP and E/e′. Obesity and AF strongly influence the result and can themselves contribute to disability. Combine probability with symptoms, imaging, laboratory findings and alternative-diagnosis assessment; use targeted functional or invasive testing when residual uncertainty would change treatment.

H2FPEF component | Original criterion | Points

Heavy | BMI >30 kg/m² | 2

Hypertensive | Treatment with ≥2 antihypertensives | 1

AF | Paroxysmal or persistent AF | 3

Pulmonary hypertension | Echo-estimated PASP >35 mmHg | 1

Elder | Age >60 years | 1

Filling pressure | E/e′ >9 | 1

An intermediate probability in the original diagnostic framework: The original score classifies 2–5 as intermediate and 6–9 as high probability. A score of eight therefore belongs to the high group, even though further testing may still be appropriate if findings are discordant.

A high predicted risk of developing HFpEF over the next five years: The score estimates whether HFpEF currently explains otherwise unexplained dyspnea. It is not a prospective five-year incidence model, although several components also contribute to future cardiovascular risk.

Invasive confirmation of HFpEF equivalent to an abnormal exercise wedge pressure: The score was derived against invasive physiological assessment but does not itself measure filling pressures. A high estimated probability is not interchangeable with a technically valid invasive confirmation in a patient with consequential residual uncertainty.

questions.question: A patient has persistent exertional dyspnea, LVEF 60% and no significant valve disease or convincing alternative explanation. A correctly calculated resting HFA–PEFF score is 3. What is the next step in the original HFA–PEFF algorithm?
options: Resting right-heart catheterization without an exercise component
Cardiac MRI for etiological characterization before functional confirmation
Functional assessment with exercise echocardiography or appropriately selected invasive exercise hemodynamics
Repeat resting natriuretic peptide and echocardiography after three months
questions.explanation:
Intermediate HFA–PEFF Results Require Functional Assessment

Correct answer: Functional assessment with exercise echocardiography or appropriately selected invasive exercise hemodynamics

Three Domains With Limited Contributions

**The original HFA–PEFF echocardiographic/biomarker step combines functional, morphological and natriuretic-peptide domains.** A major criterion contributes two points and a minor criterion one.

Each domain contributes at most two points, even when several criteria in that domain are positive. The resting score therefore ranges from zero to six.

A total of at least five supports HFpEF, zero to one makes it unlikely, and two to four requires further assessment. Use the appropriate rhythm-specific biomarker criteria rather than treating AF and sinus rhythm identically.

Resolve Exercise-Related Uncertainty

**Step F1 examines whether exertion produces pathological filling-pressure behavior.** Exercise echocardiography can assess the diastolic response when acquisition is adequate.

If noninvasive exercise assessment is inconclusive, technically unsuitable or discordant with the clinical presentation, invasive exercise hemodynamics can clarify the diagnosis at an experienced center.

Do not regard a normal resting EF or a nondiagnostic resting peptide as proof of normal exercise physiology. Conversely, an intermediate score should not automatically trigger invasive testing in every patient without considering test feasibility, alternative causes and whether the result would change care. After establishing the syndrome, investigate its etiology and relevant comorbidities rather than treating a positive score as the complete diagnosis.

HFA–PEFF domain | Major: 2 points | Minor: 1 point

Functional | Age <75: septal e′ <7 or lateral e′ <10 cm/s; age ≥75: <5 or <7 respectively; OR mean E/e′ ≥15; OR TR velocity >2.8 m/s | Mean E/e′ 9–14 OR absolute GLS <16%

Morphological | LAVI >34 mL/m² in sinus rhythm or >40 in AF; OR LVMI ≥149 (men)/122 (women) g/m² AND RWT >0.42 | LAVI 29–34 in sinus rhythm or 34–40 in AF; OR LVMI >115 (men)/95 (women) g/m²; OR RWT >0.42; OR LV wall ≥12 mm

Biomarker: sinus rhythm | NT-proBNP >220 OR BNP >80 pg/mL | NT-proBNP 125–220 OR BNP 35–80 pg/mL

Biomarker: AF | NT-proBNP >660 OR BNP >240 pg/mL | NT-proBNP 375–660 OR BNP 105–240 pg/mL

Total: maximum 2/domain | 5–6: HFpEF supported; 0–1: unlikely | 2–4: functional testing; do not add major and minor within one domain

Resting right-heart catheterization without an exercise component: Elevated resting filling pressure can confirm a hemodynamic abnormality, but a normal resting result may miss exertional HFpEF. The functional step should address the exercise-limited presentation rather than stop at resting measurements alone.

Cardiac MRI for etiological characterization before functional confirmation: CMR can identify a specific cardiomyopathic or infiltrative cause, particularly with suggestive imaging or clinical findings. At the intermediate HFA–PEFF step, the unresolved issue is exercise-related filling-pressure abnormality; etiological characterization follows or accompanies confirmation as indicated.

Repeat resting natriuretic peptide and echocardiography after three months: Repeat resting assessment may suit surveillance or a temporarily confounded initial study. Here the resting score is correctly measured and intermediate, so the algorithm calls for functional assessment rather than simply repeating the same resting evidence.

questions.question: A stable patient has newly recognized global LV systolic dysfunction with EF 30%. Coronary evaluation shows no obstructive disease, echocardiography excludes important valve disease and routine laboratory testing is unrevealing. There is no shock, sustained ventricular arrhythmia or high-grade AV block. Which next investigation most usefully characterizes the myocardial substrate?
options: Endomyocardial biopsy as the next investigation before noninvasive tissue assessment
Cardiac MRI with appropriate tissue-characterization sequences
Cardiac FDG-PET with inflammation-directed preparation
A broad cardiomyopathy genetic panel as the initial substrate investigation
questions.explanation:
Investigate the Cause of Newly Identified LV Dysfunction

Correct answer: Cardiac MRI with appropriate tissue-characterization sequences

A Syndrome Label Does Not Identify Its Cause

**Reduced EF describes ventricular dysfunction but does not establish etiology.** The initial assessment should include history, examination, ECG, echo, relevant laboratory studies and a proportionate ischemic evaluation.

Review cardiotoxic drugs, alcohol, persistent tachyarrhythmia, pregnancy-related timing, endocrine/metabolic disease and family history. A three-generation pedigree and genetic assessment may be appropriate when inherited cardiomyopathy is suspected.

Treat congestion and initiate indicated HF care while investigation proceeds. An etiological workup is not a reason to leave a stable patient untreated.

Choose a Test That Can Change Management

**CMR combines ventricular quantification with scar, edema and other tissue assessment.** Patterns can support ischemic injury, inflammation, infiltrative disease or another cardiomyopathic substrate.

A CMR pattern is not infallible proof of a specific histology. Image quality, timing, contraindications and the clinical presentation influence its diagnostic value.

Reserve endomyocardial biopsy for selected situations in which histology can alter treatment, weighing sampling limitations and procedural risks. Rapid deterioration, malignant arrhythmia or conduction disease can change the urgency and choice of investigation. Avoid applying either routine biopsy or routine invasive hemodynamic monitoring to every new low EF; select the investigation that answers the unresolved consequential question.

Endomyocardial biopsy as the next investigation before noninvasive tissue assessment: Biopsy is valuable when a suspected histological diagnosis would change treatment, particularly selected high-risk or progressive presentations. The stable scenario does not establish a reason to bypass noninvasive characterization for routine sampling.

Cardiac FDG-PET with inflammation-directed preparation: FDG-PET can assess active inflammation in selected suspected cardiac sarcoidosis and help monitor treatment. Without a specific inflammatory phenotype, CMR offers broader initial myocardial characterization rather than immediately selecting a targeted metabolic investigation.

A broad cardiomyopathy genetic panel as the initial substrate investigation: Genetic testing is valuable with an inherited phenotype, family history or when genotype changes counseling and management. It complements clinical and imaging phenotyping; in this uncharacterized sporadic presentation, it does not replace initial myocardial tissue imaging.

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

ESC heart failure guideline, 2021: conventional diagnostic thresholds — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab368

questions.question: A newly diagnosed patient with symptomatic HF and EF 28% is now euvolemic, warm and stable, with BP 122/76 mmHg, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.3 mmol/L. No major contraindication to the four foundational classes is identified. Which initiation strategy best matches the ACC 2024 pathway?
options: Introduce ARNI, MRA and SGLT2 therapy, deferring beta blockade until the three-month EF review
Introduce ARNI and beta blocker, then add MRA and SGLT2 therapy after target doses are reached
Introduce the complementary foundational classes promptly at tolerated doses, with monitoring and subsequent titration
Introduce ARNI, beta blocker and SGLT2 therapy, reserving MRA for persistent NYHA III symptoms
questions.explanation:
Establish Complementary Therapies Before Prolonged Single-Drug Titration

Correct answer: Introduce the complementary foundational classes promptly at tolerated doses, with monitoring and subsequent titration

Complementary Treatment Effects

**The ACC 2024 HFrEF core regimen comprises an ARNI, an evidence-based beta blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor.** Use an appropriate renin–angiotensin alternative when ARNI cannot be used.

No single mandatory sequence applies to every patient. Hemodynamics, congestion, kidney function, potassium, rhythm and contraindications guide initiation.

Starting tolerated doses across the indicated classes is generally preferable to spending months maximizing only one or two. Aim for target or maximally tolerated doses as soon as feasible, ideally within three months under this pathway.

Stabilization and Monitoring

**Rapid initiation means planned, monitored treatment rather than starting every medicine regardless of clinical state.** Initiate and increase beta blockade after compensation, not during hypoperfusion or escalating decompensation.

Review blood pressure, pulse, weight, symptoms, renal function and electrolytes after changes. MRA and SGLT2 therapy often have less pressure-lowering effect than other components, which can inform an individualized sequence.

Reassess loop requirements as congestion improves. Explain the purpose of each medicine and arrange early follow-up to address adherence and tolerability. A modest renal change does not automatically require stopping all prognostic treatment; interpret its magnitude, trajectory, volume status and competing causes. Record a specific contraindication when a class is omitted rather than allowing an incomplete regimen to persist without reassessment.

Introduce ARNI, MRA and SGLT2 therapy, deferring beta blockade until the three-month EF review: Deferring beta blockade is appropriate during unresolved hypoperfusion or active instability. This patient is compensated and warm; the later EF reassessment is not a prerequisite for beginning an indicated evidence-based beta blocker.

Introduce ARNI and beta blocker, then add MRA and SGLT2 therapy after target doses are reached: This traditional sequential approach may be needed when tolerance or monitoring constrains treatment. In the eligible stable patient supplied, waiting for target doses unnecessarily postpones the complementary benefits of the other classes.

Introduce ARNI, beta blocker and SGLT2 therapy, reserving MRA for persistent NYHA III symptoms: MRA treatment is not limited to NYHA III residual symptoms in otherwise eligible reduced-EF HF. The supplied kidney function and potassium do not provide a reason to omit it while waiting for greater symptom severity.

questions.explanation:
ACE Inhibitor Washout Before Sacubitril/Valsartan

Correct answer: Stop enalapril and allow at least thirty-six hours before the first sacubitril/valsartan dose

Mechanism and Required Separation

**Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin while valsartan blocks the angiotensin II type-1 receptor.** Neprilysin inhibition augments endogenous vasoactive peptides; combining it with ACE inhibition increases angioedema risk.

Allow ==at least 36 hours== when switching from an ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan, and also before starting an ACE inhibitor after stopping sacubitril/valsartan.

An ARB-to-ARNI transition does not require the same ACE-specific washout, but the prior ARB must be stopped because the combination already contains valsartan.

Contraindications and Follow-Up

**A prior episode of ACE inhibitor- or ARB-related angioedema is a contraindication to sacubitril/valsartan.** A longer washout does not make that history irrelevant.

Review pregnancy, blood pressure, renal function, potassium and interacting medicines before prescribing. Avoid duplicating renin–angiotensin blockade and select the starting dose from prior treatment and patient tolerance.

Explain urgent evaluation for swelling of the tongue, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing. Monitor for hypotension, hyperkalemia and renal deterioration after initiation and titration. A patient who develops intolerance needs reassessment of volume status, interacting drugs and a suitable alternative rather than automatic overlap with the previous ACE inhibitor. The essential transition rule is independent of whether the eventual ARNI starting dose is low or standard.

Stop enalapril and begin sacubitril/valsartan twelve hours later: A twelve-hour interval does not meet the required ACE inhibitor washout; concurrent effects on vasoactive peptide breakdown increase angioedema risk.

Stop enalapril and begin sacubitril/valsartan twenty-four hours later: A one-day interruption remains shorter than the specified thirty-six-hour minimum. The usual dosing interval of the ACE inhibitor does not define an adequate washout.

Overlap reduced-dose enalapril with sacubitril/valsartan during initial titration: Concomitant ACE inhibition and sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated. Lowering either dose does not create a validated overlap strategy or remove the angioedema hazard.

FDA Entresto prescribing information, 2024 — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/218591Orig1s000%2C207620Orig1s025lbl.pdf

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

questions.question: A stable, euvolemic patient with symptomatic HF and EF 30% has not previously taken an ACE inhibitor or ARB. BP is 116/72 mmHg, eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.4 mmol/L. Sacubitril/valsartan is selected. Which starting regimen matches the adult prescribing information?
options: Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily
Sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily
Sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily
Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg once daily
questions.explanation:
Select the Reduced ARNI Starting Dose for Minimal Prior RAS Exposure

Correct answer: Sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily

Match Starting Dose to Exposure and Tolerance

**The adult label recommends half the usual starting dose when the patient is not taking an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or was taking only a low dose.** This corresponds to ==24/26 mg twice daily==.

The usual starting regimen is 49/51 mg twice daily. Severe renal impairment, eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², also warrants half the usual starting dose under the label; the eGFR of 48 alone does not create that severe-renal category.

Assess baseline blood pressure and volume status. Correct important volume depletion and avoid assuming that a normal creatinine excludes susceptibility to hypotension.

Titrate and Monitor

**Double the dose every two to four weeks toward ==97/103 mg twice daily== as tolerated.** The target is not a requirement to escalate despite symptomatic hypotension, hyperkalemia or significant renal deterioration.

Recheck pressure, orthostatic symptoms, creatinine/eGFR and potassium after initiation and dose changes. Review diuretic requirements and other pressure-lowering or potassium-raising drugs.

Each tablet strength lists sacubitril and valsartan separately; do not confuse a combined strength with the valsartan dose alone or replace the formulation milligram-for-milligram with ordinary valsartan. Continue the other indicated foundational classes while titrating safely. A reduced starting dose is a route to sustainable treatment, not an instruction to leave the patient indefinitely at the initial dose without reassessment.

Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily: This is the usual adult starting dose when no dose-reduction circumstance applies. Lack of prior ACE inhibitor or ARB exposure calls for half that usual starting dose.

Sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily: This is the target maintenance dose, not an appropriate initial regimen in a treatment-naive patient; initiation must account for hypotension and renal/potassium effects.

Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg once daily: Reducing frequency is not the labeled adult low-start strategy. The lower-strength twice-daily regimen preserves the intended dosing schedule.

FDA Entresto prescribing information, 2024 — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/218591Orig1s000%2C207620Orig1s025lbl.pdf

ACC HFrEF treatment consensus pathway, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.12.024

questions.question: A patient hospitalized with HF and EF 25% is now euvolemic and clinically stable, without inotropes, hypoperfusion, important bradycardia or AV block. There is no prior beta-blocker treatment. Which initial prescription uses an evidence-based agent, formulation and starting dose under AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022?
options: Bisoprolol 10 mg once daily
Metoprolol tartrate 12.5 mg twice daily
Metoprolol succinate extended release 12.5 mg once daily
Carvedilol 25 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
Use an Evidence-Based Beta Blocker After Compensation

Correct answer: Metoprolol succinate extended release 12.5 mg once daily

Evidence Is Agent and Formulation Specific

**AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 identifies bisoprolol, carvedilol and sustained-release metoprolol succinate as mortality-proven HFrEF beta blockers.** Select one rather than assuming a class effect for every beta blocker.

Metoprolol succinate starts at ==12.5–25 mg once daily== and targets ==200 mg once daily== when tolerated. Bisoprolol starts at ==1.25 mg once daily== and targets ==10 mg once daily==.

Carvedilol starts at ==3.125 mg twice daily==; guideline target doses are 25–50 mg twice daily depending on patient characteristics and tolerance. Its alpha-1 blockade can affect pressure tolerance.

Initiation Is Different From Continuation During Illness

**Begin at low dose after clinical compensation and increase with reassessment.** Starting or increasing treatment during shock, active hypoperfusion or an escalating inotrope requirement can worsen hemodynamics.

Monitor heart rate, pressure, congestion, fatigue and conduction. Symptomatic bradycardia, significant AV block and active bronchospasm require individualized assessment and may limit selection or dosing.

A patient already receiving a beta blocker is a different decision from a treatment-naive patient: do not routinely withdraw chronic treatment for every admission, but reassess when shock or another major contraindication occurs. Early fatigue is not by itself proof of permanent intolerance. Aim for a tolerated evidence-based regimen alongside other foundational therapies rather than escalating solely to achieve a numerical pulse target.

Bisoprolol 10 mg once daily: Bisoprolol is an evidence-based agent, but 10 mg daily is its target dose rather than the treatment-naive starting dose. Initiation generally uses 1.25 mg daily followed by tolerated titration.

Metoprolol tartrate 12.5 mg twice daily: Short-acting tartrate can be used for other clinical purposes, but is not interchangeable with the sustained-release succinate regimen carrying the specified HFrEF mortality evidence. A low dose does not remove the formulation distinction.

Carvedilol 25 mg twice daily: Carvedilol is an evidence-based agent, but 25 mg twice daily is a target-level regimen. A treatment-naive compensated patient generally starts at 3.125 mg twice daily and increases gradually with reassessment.

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

ACC HFrEF treatment consensus pathway, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.12.024

questions.question: A patient with NYHA II HF and EF 30% is receiving tolerated foundational treatment without an MRA. Repeat potassium is 5.2 mmol/L and eGFR is 42 mL/min/1.73 m². Under AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 guidance, which plan is appropriate?
options: Start eplerenone 25 mg on alternate days with a potassium check in one week
Start spironolactone 12.5 mg daily with a potassium check in one week
Address reversible hyperkalemia and repeat laboratory assessment before starting an MRA
Replace the RAS inhibitor with an MRA after stopping the former
questions.explanation:
MRA Initiation Requires Both Renal and Potassium Eligibility

Correct answer: Address reversible hyperkalemia and repeat laboratory assessment before starting an MRA

Apply Both Initiation Conditions

**AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 recommends spironolactone or eplerenone in eligible symptomatic HFrEF when ==eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m²== and ==potassium <5.0 mmol/L==.** This patient satisfies only the renal condition.

Verify the sample and review potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, NSAIDs, trimethoprim and concurrent renin–angiotensin treatment. Identify acute kidney injury or volume disturbances.

Do not automatically withdraw all beneficial medicines from a single modest elevation. Correct contributors and use a monitored reassessment plan.

Dosing and Surveillance After Eligibility Is Established

**Spironolactone commonly starts at 12.5–25 mg daily, with target 25–50 mg daily; eplerenone commonly starts at 25 mg daily, targeting 50 mg daily.** Reduced renal function may require a lower or alternate-day starting regimen.

The named guideline advises renal and potassium checks approximately one week and four weeks after initiation or intensification, then about every six months when stable; test more often with instability or increased risk.

If potassium cannot be maintained ==below 5.5 mmol/L== during treatment, discontinue the MRA under this framework to avoid life-threatening hyperkalemia. Initiation and continuation thresholds are different decisions. Spironolactone can cause gynecomastia or breast discomfort; eplerenone may be selected for those effects but still requires renal, potassium and interaction review. Document a follow-up date so temporary deferral does not become an unexamined permanent treatment gap.

Start eplerenone 25 mg on alternate days with a potassium check in one week: An alternate-day regimen can be appropriate with reduced renal function in an otherwise eligible patient. Eplerenone still raises potassium, so agent selection and a lower frequency do not remove the current initiation barrier.

Start spironolactone 12.5 mg daily with a potassium check in one week: Low-dose spironolactone with early surveillance can be appropriate after initiation criteria are met. Renal eligibility does not cancel the requirement for potassium below 5.0 mmol/L; monitoring cannot substitute for correcting the current elevation first.

Replace the RAS inhibitor with an MRA after stopping the former: Replacing one indicated class is not the default response to modest hyperkalemia. The current potassium level also constrains MRA initiation, so contributors and repeat values should be assessed before restructuring the complementary regimen.

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

ACC HFrEF treatment consensus pathway, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.12.024

questions.question: A stable patient with symptomatic HF and EF 32% has HbA1c 5.5%, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m² and no volume depletion. Dapagliflozin is being considered for HF. Which plan is appropriate under its US prescribing information?
options: Start dapagliflozin 10 mg on alternate days
Start dapagliflozin 5 mg once daily
Start dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily
Defer initiation until eGFR is at least 45 mL/min/1.73 m²
questions.explanation:
SGLT2 Treatment for HF Does Not Require Diabetes

Correct answer: Start dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily

Indication and Renal Context

**Dapagliflozin inhibits proximal tubular SGLT2 and has an adult HF indication independent of diabetes.** Its clinical use in HF is not simply glucose lowering in a patient with an abnormal HbA1c.

The HF dose is ==10 mg once daily==. Under the cited US label, initiation is not recommended below ==eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73 m²==; patients already treated may continue below that threshold for the specified cardiorenal indications.

Assess renal function and correct volume depletion before starting. Glycemic-control restrictions should not be substituted for the separate HF dosing instructions.

Anticipate Preventable Adverse Events

**Counsel about genital fungal infection, volume depletion and ketoacidosis that may occur without marked hyperglycemia.** Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or unexplained breathlessness warrant assessment rather than reassurance from a near-normal glucose.

Withhold dapagliflozin for ==at least three days==, if possible, before surgery or procedures involving prolonged fasting. Restart when clinically stable and oral intake has resumed; acute illness or prolonged poor intake may require temporary interruption.

Review concurrent diuretics and symptoms of orthostasis. A small early eGFR dip can be hemodynamic, but progressive deterioration requires assessment for hypovolemia, illness and other causes. Avoid assuming that the absence of diabetes abolishes every adverse-effect risk. Provide a clear sick-day and restart plan while preserving the purpose of long-term HF treatment.

Start dapagliflozin 10 mg on alternate days: Alternate-day dosing may appear a cautious response to CKD, but it is not the labeled HF regimen. At eGFR 38, use the indicated daily dose after assessing volume status and other safety considerations.

Start dapagliflozin 5 mg once daily: A 5-mg starting dose is used for glycemic control in eligible patients, but the adult HF regimen is 10 mg daily. Kidney function of 38 does not require a lower HF starting dose under the cited label.

Defer initiation until eGFR is at least 45 mL/min/1.73 m²: The eGFR 45 limitation concerns glycemic efficacy rather than the separate HF indication. The cited US label permits initiation for HF at this patient’s eGFR, with renal and volume monitoring.

questions.explanationHtml:
SGLT2 Treatment for HF Does Not Require Diabetes

Correct answer: C — Start dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily

Indication and Renal Context

  • Dapagliflozin inhibits proximal tubular SGLT2 and has an adult HF indication independent of diabetes. Its clinical use in HF is not simply glucose lowering in a patient with an abnormal HbA1c.
    • The HF dose is 10 mg once daily. Under the cited US label, initiation is not recommended below eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73 m²; patients already treated may continue below that threshold for the specified cardiorenal indications.
    • Assess renal function and correct volume depletion before starting. Glycemic-control restrictions should not be substituted for the separate HF dosing instructions.

Anticipate Preventable Adverse Events

  • Counsel about genital fungal infection, volume depletion and ketoacidosis that may occur without marked hyperglycemia. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or unexplained breathlessness warrant assessment rather than reassurance from a near-normal glucose.
    • Withhold dapagliflozin for at least three days, if possible, before surgery or procedures involving prolonged fasting. Restart when clinically stable and oral intake has resumed; acute illness or prolonged poor intake may require temporary interruption.
    • Review concurrent diuretics and symptoms of orthostasis. A small early eGFR dip can be hemodynamic, but progressive deterioration requires assessment for hypovolemia, illness and other causes. Avoid assuming that the absence of diabetes abolishes every adverse-effect risk. Provide a clear sick-day and restart plan while preserving the purpose of long-term HF treatment.

Other Options

  • A — Start dapagliflozin 10 mg on alternate days: Alternate-day dosing may appear a cautious response to CKD, but it is not the labeled HF regimen. At eGFR 38, use the indicated daily dose after assessing volume status and other safety considerations.
  • B — Start dapagliflozin 5 mg once daily: A 5-mg starting dose is used for glycemic control in eligible patients, but the adult HF regimen is 10 mg daily. Kidney function of 38 does not require a lower HF starting dose under the cited label.
  • D — Defer initiation until eGFR is at least 45 mL/min/1.73 m²: The eGFR 45 limitation concerns glycemic efficacy rather than the separate HF indication. The cited US label permits initiation for HF at this patient’s eGFR, with renal and volume monitoring.

  • FDA dapagliflozin prescribing information, 2026
  • AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022
  • ACC HFrEF treatment consensus pathway, 2024

questions.question: A stable patient with EF 28% develops mild orthostatic dizziness after treatment changes. Seated BP is 100/64 mmHg, with a symptomatic postural fall. Pulse is 76/min; the patient is warm, euvolemic and has stable renal function and potassium. Medicines include sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, dapagliflozin and amlodipine prescribed solely for previous hypertension. No loop diuretic is required. Which medication should be reviewed for withdrawal first?
options: Sacubitril/valsartan
Carvedilol
Spironolactone
Amlodipine
questions.explanation:
Review Nonessential Pressure-Lowering Treatment Before Abandoning HF Therapy

Correct answer: Amlodipine

Assess Symptoms, Perfusion and Volume

**A low pressure reading is not equivalent to cardiogenic shock.** Determine whether symptoms correlate with orthostasis and assess mentation, peripheral perfusion, urine output and congestion.

Look for diarrhea, poor intake, recent diuretic escalation, infection and other reversible causes. Review all prescriptions, including alpha blockers, nitrates and drugs prescribed outside the HF clinic.

A patient with cool extremities, oliguria or worsening organ function needs urgent evaluation; the stable scenario here supports a deliberate medication review.

Preserve Complementary Outcome Benefit

**Remove or reduce pressure-lowering treatment without a current compelling indication when feasible.** Amlodipine can treat hypertension or angina but is not a foundational HFrEF outcome therapy.

If there is no congestion, reassess whether the loop dose remains necessary. Persistent symptomatic hypotension may still require individualized adjustment of HF medicines; do not force target doses despite intolerance.

When possible, retain tolerated doses from complementary classes rather than maximizing one while eliminating the others. Bradycardia, renal dysfunction and hyperkalemia can change which medicine is adjusted. Recheck standing pressure and symptoms after intervention and document a plan to reassess temporarily reduced treatment. This sequence is patient-specific and does not make every antihypertensive dispensable when a separate indication remains.

Sacubitril/valsartan: ARNI can contribute to hypotension and may require dose adjustment if symptoms persist. However, it has an HF outcome indication, whereas amlodipine has no remaining compelling indication in the supplied patient.

Carvedilol: Reducing beta blockade can be necessary with symptomatic bradycardia or persistent intolerance after reversible causes are addressed. Pulse is 76/min, perfusion is preserved and a nonessential pressure-lowering drug remains, favoring preservation of carvedilol initially.

Spironolactone: MRA reduction may be necessary with hyperkalemia, significant renal deterioration or persisting intolerance. Its pressure effect at HF doses is relatively modest and those limiting findings are absent, so it is not the first medicine to remove here.

questions.question: A patient with stable HFrEF and CKD starts an ACE inhibitor because ARNI is not feasible. Two weeks later, creatinine has risen from 1.5 to 1.8 mg/dL and is stable on repeat testing. Potassium is 4.6 mmol/L, BP 116/70 mmHg, and there is no hypovolemia or new illness. Which approach best fits KDIGO 2024 guidance?
options: Interrupt the ACE inhibitor and repeat renal testing after one week
Continue the ACE inhibitor with planned renal and potassium monitoring
Halve the ACE inhibitor dose and maintain the reduced dose
Replace the ACE inhibitor with an ARB to prevent the filtration change
questions.explanation:
A Modest Creatinine Rise After ACE Inhibition Requires Context

Correct answer: Continue the ACE inhibitor with planned renal and potassium monitoring

Recognize the Hemodynamic Effect

**ACE inhibition reduces angiotensin-mediated efferent arteriolar tone and can lower intraglomerular pressure.** Serum creatinine may increase without direct tubular toxicity.

The change here is (1.8−1.5)/1.5 ×100 = 20%. KDIGO 2024 advises continuing ACE inhibitor or ARB unless creatinine rises by ==more than 30% within four weeks== of initiation or dose increase.

This is an ACEi/ARB practice point in CKD, not a universal permission to ignore renal deterioration on every HF medicine or during shock.

Identify Findings That Change the Plan

**Check pressure, potassium, volume status and the direction of change.** A progressive rise, symptomatic hypotension or uncontrolled hyperkalemia warrants reassessment and may require dose reduction or interruption.

Review NSAIDs, diuretic-related depletion, sepsis, obstruction and possible renovascular disease when appropriate. A larger early rise should trigger investigation rather than being attributed automatically to benign adaptation.

KDIGO recommends checking pressure, creatinine and potassium within two to four weeks after starting or increasing ACEi/ARB, with timing individualized to baseline risk. HF or unstable patients may require earlier checks. Continue longitudinal surveillance after an initially acceptable result. Preserving indicated treatment and recognizing genuine acute kidney injury are compatible goals when decisions follow the full clinical picture.

Interrupt the ACE inhibitor and repeat renal testing after one week: Interruption can be necessary with progressive renal deterioration, significant hypotension or uncontrolled hyperkalemia. A stable 20% rise with acceptable pressure and potassium does not meet the cited creatinine trigger for routine interruption.

Halve the ACE inhibitor dose and maintain the reduced dose: Dose reduction may be appropriate when adverse effects persist after contributors are addressed. Here the change is within the cited acceptable early range, so automatic dose reduction sacrifices indicated treatment without a supplied intolerance.

Replace the ACE inhibitor with an ARB to prevent the filtration change: An ARB may substitute for ACE-inhibitor cough or other appropriate intolerance. Both reduce angiotensin-mediated efferent arteriolar tone, so changing classes does not inherently eliminate this hemodynamic filtration response.

questions.question: A patient with HFrEF has recurrent treatment-limiting hyperkalemia despite correction of supplements and other reversible causes. The HF team considers patiromer to facilitate renin–angiotensin–aldosterone inhibitor treatment. Which interpretation of DIAMOND and AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 guidance is most accurate?
options: DIAMOND randomized unselected patients before testing tolerance of RAAS inhibitor optimization
DIAMOND established reduced cardiovascular mortality as its definitive primary result
DIAMOND found potassium lowering but no improvement in maintaining MRA treatment
Patiromer can improve potassium control and treatment maintenance, but this does not establish an independent mortality benefit
questions.explanation:
Potassium Control and Proven HF Outcome Benefit Are Different Endpoints

Correct answer: Patiromer can improve potassium control and treatment maintenance, but this does not establish an independent mortality benefit

Interpret the Trial as Conducted

**DIAMOND evaluated patiromer in HFrEF with current or previous RAAS inhibitor-related hyperkalemia.** A run-in phase combined binder treatment with optimization before randomized withdrawal to patiromer or placebo.

The final primary endpoint was the adjusted mean change in potassium. Patiromer improved potassium control and reduced recurrent hyperkalemia and MRA dose-reduction events.

The selected run-in population and changed primary endpoint matter when judging generalizability. This study does not establish that the binder itself reduces mortality.

Build a Safe Treatment-Retention Plan

**Treat the degree and urgency of hyperkalemia before deciding long-term drug retention.** Review ECG and clinical context when indicated, kidney function, interacting medicines, supplements and dietary potassium sources.

AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 described improved clinical outcomes from binder-facilitated RAAS inhibitor continuation as uncertain. Distinguish that uncertainty from evidence that binders can lower potassium.

Patiromer is not a substitute for emergency treatment of life-threatening hyperkalemia. Ongoing treatment requires attention to gastrointestinal tolerance, magnesium and separation from interacting oral medicines according to its label. If potassium cannot be maintained within a safe range, adjust or interrupt the implicated therapy and reassess. A monitored strategy should preserve appropriate HF benefit without treating the desire to maintain a medicine as a reason to disregard unsafe laboratory results.

DIAMOND randomized unselected patients before testing tolerance of RAAS inhibitor optimization: The study used a run-in incorporating patiromer and RAAS inhibitor optimization before randomized withdrawal. That selection affects generalizability to patients unable to complete optimization and differs from an unselected initiation trial.

DIAMOND established reduced cardiovascular mortality as its definitive primary result: The trial’s final primary endpoint was change in serum potassium, after alteration of the original outcome plan. Improved potassium-related results cannot be relabeled as a proven mortality reduction.

DIAMOND found potassium lowering but no improvement in maintaining MRA treatment: The trial assessed more than a laboratory difference: patiromer reduced MRA dose-reduction events as well as recurrent hyperkalemia. That treatment-maintenance finding should be preserved without inflating it into a mortality claim.

questions.question: An asymptomatic patient previously treated for dilated cardiomyopathy now has normalized LV dimensions and EF 56%. There is no medication intolerance. The patient asks to stop all HF medicines because the heart has recovered. Which response best reflects TRED-HF and guideline recommendations?
options: Continue the beta blocker but withdraw the renin–angiotensin inhibitor
Offer phased withdrawal with scheduled imaging and biomarker surveillance
Continue indicated HF therapy because remission does not reliably identify a group safe for routine withdrawal
Reduce disease-modifying therapy to initial doses for long-term maintenance
questions.explanation:
TRED-HF Supports Continued Therapy After Remission

Correct answer: Continue indicated HF therapy because remission does not reliably identify a group safe for routine withdrawal

The Trial Tested Withdrawal in Apparent Recovery

**TRED-HF was an open-label randomized pilot study in recovered dilated cardiomyopathy.** Participants had improved function and favorable clinical and structural findings before withdrawal was considered.

Within the first six months, 11 of 25 patients assigned to phased withdrawal relapsed, compared with none of 26 assigned initially to continued treatment: 44% versus 0%.

The endpoint captured objective deterioration as well as clinical recurrence. It was not simply a comparison of deaths or symptomatic hospital admissions.

Apply Remission Evidence Without Overgeneralization

**AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 recommends continuing treatment in HF with improved EF to prevent relapse, even when symptoms resolve.** Improvement can reflect the benefit of therapy rather than disappearance of susceptibility.

TRED-HF does not prove that every medicine has identical withdrawal risk in every etiology, nor does it eliminate individualized adjustment for adverse effects. It does argue against routine wholesale cessation based on one normal scan.

Discuss adherence, pregnancy plans, competing illnesses and tolerability. Follow symptoms, function and relevant imaging or biomarkers as clinically indicated. Loop-diuretic reduction in a persistently euvolemic patient is a different decision from stopping the disease-modifying regimen. If treatment must be interrupted, document why, monitor closely and revisit reintroduction rather than describing remission as a permanent cure.

Continue the beta blocker but withdraw the renin–angiotensin inhibitor: Selective withdrawal may become necessary for a specific adverse effect or contraindication. Neither the normalized EF nor TRED-HF establishes that this particular residual regimen safely preserves remission in a patient without intolerance.

Offer phased withdrawal with scheduled imaging and biomarker surveillance: The TRED-HF withdrawal strategy included structured surveillance yet relapse was common. Monitoring can detect deterioration but does not establish that routine withdrawal is safe in an asymptomatic patient tolerating treatment.

Reduce disease-modifying therapy to initial doses for long-term maintenance: Dose reduction can address intolerance after individual assessment. There is no supplied intolerance and the trial does not validate routine de-escalation to starting doses merely because ventricular dimensions and EF have normalized.

TRED-HF randomized pilot trial, 2018 online/2019 print — https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32484-X

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063

Discuss adherence, pregnancy plans, competing illnesses and tolerability. Follow symptoms, function and relevant imaging or biomarkers as clinically indicated. Loop-diuretic reduction in a persistently euvolemic patient is a different decision from stopping the disease-modifying regimen. If treatment must be interrupted, document why, monitor closely and revisit reintroduction rather than describing remission as a permanent cure.

otherOptions.explanation: Selective withdrawal may become necessary for a specific adverse effect or contraindication. Neither the normalized EF nor TRED-HF establishes that this particular residual regimen safely preserves remission in a patient without intolerance.

The TRED-HF withdrawal strategy included structured surveillance yet relapse was common. Monitoring can detect deterioration but does not establish that routine withdrawal is safe in an asymptomatic patient tolerating treatment.

Dose reduction can address intolerance after individual assessment. There is no supplied intolerance and the trial does not validate routine de-escalation to starting doses merely because ventricular dimensions and EF have normalized.

questions.question: A patient with HFrEF remains well perfused and euvolemic after several weeks of stable weight and examination. Foundational treatment is tolerated. Furosemide is still being taken at the higher dose used during a recent congestive episode. What is the most appropriate prescribing principle?
options: Retain the admission loop dose until the next EF reassessment
Reassess and use the lowest loop dose that maintains euvolemia while continuing indicated foundational treatment
Convert the loop to symptom-triggered treatment immediately
Switch to torsemide to provide a proven survival advantage
questions.explanation:
Loop Diuretics Are Titrated to Congestion Rather Than a Prognostic Target Dose

Correct answer: Reassess and use the lowest loop dose that maintains euvolemia while continuing indicated foundational treatment

Mechanism and Treatment Goal

**Loop diuretics inhibit the Na–K–2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb and relieve sodium and water retention.** Their practical dose depends on congestion, kidney function, absorption and the observed response.

AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 lists oral furosemide 20–40 mg once or twice daily as a common initial regimen. Established patients may require substantially different doses, which should not be copied from a generic starting range.

The aim is sustained euvolemia, not the maximum possible urine output or routine escalation to a fixed high dose.

Reduce Excess Exposure Without Inviting Recurrent Congestion

**Review symptoms, weight trend, orthostasis, venous pressure, edema, renal function and electrolytes before adjustment.** Some patients need continuing maintenance treatment to avoid recurrent fluid retention.

Monitor sodium, potassium and magnesium, especially with combination diuretics. Hypokalemia can increase arrhythmic and digoxin-related risk; excessive diuresis can produce hypotension and renal dysfunction.

Provide an individualized weight and symptom action plan and a review date after dose changes. Do not assume one normal visit means every patient can stop diuretics permanently. Conversely, ARNI and SGLT2 treatment or improved HF status may lower loop requirements. Keep relief of congestion and outcome-modifying therapy conceptually distinct while recognizing that both are important components of care.

Retain the admission loop dose until the next EF reassessment: A recent high dose may remain necessary if congestion recurs, but EF is not the principal loop-titration target. Stable euvolemia should prompt review of dose need rather than waiting for an unrelated imaging milestone.

Convert the loop to symptom-triggered treatment immediately: Selected stable patients can use an individualized flexible or intermittent regimen after assessment. Abruptly making symptoms the only trigger can miss early recurrent congestion; maintenance needs and a weight/action plan should be reviewed first.

Switch to torsemide to provide a proven survival advantage: Torsemide may suit absorption, response or adherence considerations, but its routine replacement of furosemide has not established a survival advantage. Drug selection does not remove the need to reassess the dose required for euvolemia.

questions.question: A previously stable patient with EF 30% develops edema, rising blood pressure and reduced response to the usual loop dose after starting oral ibuprofen for joint pain. Adherence to HF medicines is confirmed. Which mechanism best explains the new deterioration?
options: Renal prostaglandin inhibition causing sodium retention and reduced diuretic responsiveness
Precapillary arteriolar dilation increasing dependent capillary hydrostatic pressure
Direct myocardial calcium-channel inhibition reducing ventricular contractility
PPAR-gamma activation promoting renal sodium retention and volume expansion
questions.explanation:
NSAID Exposure Can Blunt Diuresis and Precipitate Congestion

Correct answer: Renal prostaglandin inhibition causing sodium retention and reduced diuretic responsiveness

Recognize a Reversible Drug Trigger

**Systemic NSAIDs can worsen HF through renal prostaglandin inhibition, sodium/water retention, increased vascular resistance and reduced diuretic response.** COX-2 selectivity does not eliminate these concerns.

Review over-the-counter analgesics as well as prescription drugs. The temporal association supports a trigger but does not exclude another concurrent cause of decompensation.

Assess congestion, perfusion, kidney function and potassium promptly. Coordinate discontinuation of the precipitating drug and a safer pain-management plan while treating the HF deterioration.

Compare Other Important Drug Hazards

**Different medicines worsen HF through different mechanisms.** Avoid treating every peripheral edema or creatinine change as the same adverse effect.

Thiazolidinediones can cause fluid retention and should be avoided in symptomatic HF. Diltiazem and verapamil have negative inotropic effects and are generally unsuitable in HFrEF.

Amlodipine may be used for a separate pressure or angina indication but is not foundational HF treatment; ankle edema on it is not automatically proof of cardiogenic volume overload. Review antiarrhythmic and potassium-raising interactions according to the individual regimen. A complete medication reconciliation can identify a reversible contributor before escalating diuretics indefinitely or declaring progression despite optimal treatment.

Precapillary arteriolar dilation increasing dependent capillary hydrostatic pressure: This mechanism helps explain dihydropyridine calcium-channel-blocker ankle edema, which need not reflect generalized sodium retention. It does not best explain ibuprofen-associated pressure rise and loss of loop responsiveness.

Direct myocardial calcium-channel inhibition reducing ventricular contractility: Negative inotropy contributes to concerns with verapamil or diltiazem in reduced-EF HF. The principal supplied NSAID mechanism is altered renal prostaglandin signaling and sodium handling rather than therapeutic calcium-channel blockade.

PPAR-gamma activation promoting renal sodium retention and volume expansion: Thiazolidinediones can worsen HF through this pathway and are plausible drug-related causes of fluid retention. Ibuprofen does not act through PPAR-gamma activation; the exposure identifies prostaglandin inhibition instead.

questions.topic: Additional therapy, comorbidity and preserved EF
questions.question: A stable patient has NYHA II HF, EF 30% and sinus rhythm at 82/min despite maximally tolerated carvedilol and other indicated foundational therapy. Further beta-blocker titration causes symptomatic hypotension. Which additional treatment most directly fits the residual sinus-rate indication?
options: Vericiguat
Digoxin
Hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate
Ivabradine
questions.explanation:
Ivabradine Requires Sinus Rhythm and Residual Tachycardia

Correct answer: Ivabradine

Match the Mechanism to the Rhythm

**Ivabradine inhibits the sinoatrial If current and lowers sinus rate.** It is not a ventricular rate-control substitute for AF.

The US adult HF indication requires stable symptomatic chronic HF, LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm and resting heart rate ≥70/min despite maximally tolerated beta blockade or a beta-blocker contraindication.

The treatment aims to reduce worsening-HF hospitalization. It does not replace the broader survival evidence and complementary mechanisms of foundational therapy.

Dose, Monitoring and Interactions

**The usual adult starting dose is ==5 mg twice daily== with food.** Reassess after two weeks and adjust toward a resting rate of ==50–60/min==; the maximum is ==7.5 mg twice daily==.

Start at 2.5 mg twice daily when conduction disease or susceptibility to bradycardic compromise warrants caution. Reduce treatment for rate below 50/min or bradycardic symptoms and stop if these persist at the lowest dose.

Monitor for AF, bradycardia and luminous visual phenomena. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors are contraindicated; avoid clinically important exposure-increasing interactions such as verapamil or diltiazem. Assess conduction, pacemaker dependence, blood pressure and pregnancy risk before prescribing. New AF changes the rationale for continued therapy. A drug that lowers sinus rate is useful only when the patient matches the rhythm-specific indication and has already had an appropriate beta-blocker assessment.

Vericiguat: Vericiguat is assessed in selected worsening HF using clinical history and eligibility conditions. It does not selectively address residual sinus-rate elevation, and the stem supplies no recent worsening event to match that add-on pathway.

Digoxin: Digoxin may be considered in selected persistently symptomatic reduced-EF HF and provides ventricular rate control in selected AF. It does not match the specific sinus-rate, EF and maximally tolerated beta-blocker eligibility pattern as directly as ivabradine.

Hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate: This combination has defined add-on and RAS-intolerance indications and lowers preload and afterload. Residual sinus tachycardia alone does not establish those indications; additional vasodilation may also be limited by this patient’s pressure tolerance.

questions.question: A patient who self-identifies as African American has persistent NYHA III HFrEF despite maximally tolerated foundational treatment. BP is 126/76 mmHg. There is no PDE5 inhibitor or riociguat use and no other contraindication. Which additional vasodilator strategy matches AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 guidance?
options: Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate
Hydralazine plus isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide dinitrate alone
Hydralazine plus amlodipine
questions.explanation:
Hydralazine–Isosorbide Dinitrate Has a Defined Add-On Evidence Base

Correct answer: Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate

Preserve the Studied Population and Background Treatment

**AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 recommends hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate for self-identified African American patients with NYHA III–IV HFrEF receiving optimal therapy.** A-HeFT supports the population-specific add-on evidence.

The trial used self-identification rather than a genetic assay. Do not infer an individual response from race alone or use this evidence to withhold foundational therapy from any group.

The combination may also be considered in selected symptomatic HFrEF when ARNI, ACE inhibitor or ARB cannot be used because of intolerance or renal limitations; the evidence and recommendation strength differ.

Prescribe the Combination Safely

**The fixed-dose tablet contains hydralazine 37.5 mg and isosorbide dinitrate 20 mg.** Start one tablet three times daily and titrate as tolerated to two tablets three times daily: 75/40 mg per dose.

Hydralazine primarily reduces arterial afterload and nitrate therapy provides venodilation through nitric-oxide signaling. Headache, dizziness and hypotension can limit adherence and titration.

Nitrates must not be combined with PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat because of severe hypotension risk. Monitor pressure and symptoms, and assess hydralazine-related lupus-like illness when compatible features develop. Three-times-daily treatment creates a real adherence burden. Explain the indication and preserve tolerated foundational therapy rather than assuming symptom improvement makes the rest of the regimen unnecessary.

Hydralazine plus isosorbide mononitrate: Both drugs have vasodilator uses, but substituting mononitrate does not reproduce the specific combination tested in the population-based outcome evidence. Use the studied dinitrate regimen rather than assuming nitrate formulations are outcome-equivalent.

Isosorbide dinitrate alone: Dinitrate monotherapy can relieve angina and reduce preload, but the specified HF outcome evidence concerns its combination with hydralazine. The isolated nitrate does not reproduce complementary arterial and venous vasodilation.

Hydralazine plus amlodipine: These agents can lower arterial pressure in selected hypertension settings. Amlodipine does not replace the nitrate component of the HF outcome regimen, and a separate blood-pressure indication is not supplied.

questions.question: An older patient with HFrEF has been stable on digoxin 0.125 mg daily. After an intercurrent illness, kidney function deteriorates and amiodarone is added for a separate arrhythmic indication. Nausea and new bradycardia develop. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Reduce digoxin to alternate-day dosing and arrange a routine outpatient trough next week
Withhold digoxin pending urgent clinical, ECG, electrolyte and appropriately timed concentration assessment
Stop amiodarone alone and continue digoxin while arranging its next trough concentration
Administer digoxin-specific antibody fragments before obtaining ECG or electrolyte findings
questions.explanation:
Digoxin Exposure Must Be Reassessed When Kidney Function Declines

Correct answer: Withhold digoxin pending urgent clinical, ECG, electrolyte and appropriately timed concentration assessment

Identify Accumulation and Interactions

**Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic margin and substantial renal elimination.** Dose requirements depend on kidney function, lean body mass, age and interacting medicines.

Amiodarone can increase digoxin exposure and requires dose/frequency review with monitoring. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia increase susceptibility to adverse cardiac effects even without an extreme serum concentration.

questions.question: Which conclusion follows from the original DIGIT-HF randomized report when considering additional treatment for symptomatic reduced-EF HF?
options: Digitoxin reduced the composite of all-cause death or first worsening-HF hospitalization in the studied population, without proving identical benefit for digoxin
The trial demonstrated a statistically conclusive isolated all-cause mortality reduction
The trial validates the same milligram dose and serum target for digoxin
The trial established digitoxin as a substitute for foundational HF treatment
questions.explanation:
DIGIT-HF Tested Digitoxin Rather Than Interchangeable Glycoside Treatment

Correct answer: Digitoxin reduced the composite of all-cause death or first worsening-HF hospitalization in the studied population, without proving identical benefit for digoxin

Population and Primary Endpoint

**DIGIT-HF randomized symptomatic chronic HF patients to digitoxin or placebo on background treatment.** Eligibility included EF ≤40% with NYHA III–IV or EF ≤30% with NYHA II.

The primary endpoint was all-cause death or first hospitalization for worsening HF. In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, it occurred in 39.5% versus 44.1% over a median 36 months: HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69–0.98.

The all-cause mortality component had HR 0.86 with 95% CI 0.69–1.07. Retain the distinction between a significant composite and a component not independently established as significant.

Drug-Specific Application

**The trial started digitoxin at 0.07 mg once daily with protocol-guided adjustment.** Its target serum range was 8–18 ng/mL, substantially different from the low-concentration digoxin HF target.

Digitoxin depends less on renal elimination than digoxin, but still has a narrow therapeutic margin, important interactions and a need for clinical and laboratory surveillance. In DECISION (2026), low-dose digoxin in 1,001 patients with EF ≤50% did not significantly reduce total worsening-HF events or cardiovascular death: rate ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.61–1.07. Its population, drug and recurrent-event endpoint differ from DIGIT-HF.

Availability, local authorization, guideline interpretation and individual risk determine use. A positive add-on trial does not justify universal initiation or imply that every cardiac glycoside has identical contemporary outcome evidence. Explain potential benefit alongside adverse effects and avoid using a familiar drug name as a substitute for matching the actual trial intervention, population and monitoring protocol.

The trial demonstrated a statistically conclusive isolated all-cause mortality reduction: The primary composite was significant, but the reported mortality component confidence interval included no effect. Composite benefit cannot be renamed an established isolated survival effect.

The trial validates the same milligram dose and serum target for digoxin: The drugs have different dosing, concentration ranges and elimination characteristics. A digitoxin regimen cannot be transferred directly to digoxin.

The trial established digitoxin as a substitute for foundational HF treatment: Digitoxin was tested in addition to guideline-directed treatment, not as a replacement for the complementary therapies already indicated in HFrEF.

DECISION low-dose digoxin randomized trial, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04406-6
